catalog_quote: (p. 242) As noted in 4.1.3, a number of languages in western Indonesia also have postploded nasals word-medially, as in Narum of northern Sarawak (stress is final) [tumbáŋ] ‘to fell trees’, [məndáwʔ] ‘to bathe’, [miñʤám] ‘borrow’, or [əŋgáp] ‘scorpion’. || (p. 186) Unlike the Philippines, stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo. However, unlike much of the AN world, where stress falls predictably on the penult, many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context. Final stress thus appears to serve as a marker of decontextualised lexical data. || (p. 253) Uma Juman type For the Uma Juman dialect of Kayan in south-central Sarawak Blust (1977c) recorded a variable stress pattern that is sensitive to syntactic context: in citation forms stress is final, but in phrasal context it is penultimate ... A similar pattern, whereby final stress appears to serve as a marker of citation forms, is widespread in coastal and downriver areas of Sarawak.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened. Both passages are at the stated locators: extracted text of PDF page 284 carries the running head "242 Chapter 4" and reads "As noted in 4.1.3, a number of languages in western Indonesia also have postploded nasals word-medially, as in Narum of northern Sarawak (stress is final) [tum-áŋ] 'to fell trees', [m&ndáwʔ] 'to bathe', [miñʤám] 'borrow', or [&ŋgáp] 'scorpion'."; PDF page 228 (running head "186 Chapter 4") reads "Unlike the Philippines, stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo. However, unlike much of the AN world, where stress falls predictably on the penult, many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Narum (Narom) falls on the final syllable, per the fieldworker's own transcriptions (tumbáŋ, məndáwʔ, miñʤám, əŋgáp). Blust's general remark for Borneo: stress is non-phonemic everywhere on the island, and in many coastal Sarawak languages (Narom is one) final stress holds in citation forms while penultimate stress appears in phrasal context.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Narum. The p. 186 passage flags that final stress in coastal Sarawak languages may be a citation-form phenomenon, with penultimate stress in connected speech; it does not say whether this applies to Narum specifically.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms (disyllabic bases from fieldnotes). The general Borneo statement explicitly contrasts citation forms (final) with phrasal context (penultimate).
new_statements.identity_note: Blust writes 'Narum' = Narom (naro1251), the variety of Kampung Narum on the Baram River (Blust 2013 p. 641 area: 'Narum, a closely related language spoken some twenty five miles up the Baram River' from Miri). Aman et al. 2021 treat Narom as one of five 'Miriek' variants (Bakam, Dalek, Bakong, Narom, Kiput); Miri'/Miriek is a dialect of naro1251 in Glottolog/Ethnologue, while Kiput is a separate language (kipu1237). The statement applies to Narum proper, not specifically to the Miriek or Bakong dialects.
